summary.title: Visualizing algorithms for rate limiting
summary.one_liner: You learn how fixed window, sliding window (approximated floating window), and token bucket rate limiters work, their trade-offs, and practical rules for implementing them.
keywords: how to choose rate limiting algorithm
takeaways: A fixed window limiter counts requests per reset window and is simple and predictable, but can allow bursts up to 2x the limit around window boundaries.
A sliding window refills capacity one request at a time; an approximated (floating) window avoids storing every timestamp while staying close to the true average.
A token bucket separates burst capacity (bucket size) from long-term average rate (refill interval), so it allows bursts while enforcing an average rate.
Production concerns include a persisted store such as Redis, failing open when the store is unreachable, choosing sensible keys, and returning 429 with x-ratelimit headers.
summary.summary: The article explains why rate limiting matters, using a Twitch chat spam example and API endpoint limits, then walks through three algorithms: fixed windows (with a note on time zone and DST pitfalls and a user-defined start variant), sliding windows (including an efficient floating-window approximation used by Upstash and Cloudflare), and token buckets (with Stripe and OpenAI examples). Each section lists pros, cons, and real-world examples, with interactive visualizations. It closes with practical advice on persistence, fail-open behavior, keying, and error responses, and a short guide to choosing an algorithm.
